01.note: Rav Ashi owned a forest in Shelaniya and went to cut it down during the intermediate days of the Festival. Rav Sheila of Shelaniya asked him whether he was relying on Rav's ruling that a person may chop down a palm tree then even if he needs only its sawdust, when Abaye had cursed such behavior. Rav Ashi answered that he had not heard that, a polite way of saying he did not agree. Then his ax slipped and nearly cut off his leg. He stopped, and came back to cut the forest only after the Festival.
01.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rav's permission to chop down a palm tree on the intermediate days, and Abaye's curse on it. This story shows what happened to a Sage who acted on the lenient ruling.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who owned a forest and set out to cut it down during the Festival.

people.name: Rav Sheila from Shelaniya
people.about: A local Sage who questions Rav Ashi's tree cutting.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who cursed chopping down trees on the intermediate days for so small a need.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage whose ruling, reported by Rav Hananel, allowed cutting down a palm tree for its sawdust.

terms.meaning: The middle days of Passover and Sukkot, between the holy first and last days. Ordinary work is restricted on them, but some work is allowed to prevent a loss.

02.note: Rabbi Yannai had an orchard whose fruit became ready to harvest during the intermediate days of the Festival, and he harvested it then. The next year everyone delayed harvesting their orchards until the intermediate days. That year Rabbi Yannai declared his orchard ownerless.
02.why: The Gemara has been gathering cases of farm work on the intermediate days. Right after this, the Mishna rules that someone who plans his work for those days from the outset must lose what that work produces.

people.name: Rabbi Yannai
people.about: A Sage whose harvest during the Festival led others to put off their own harvests until then.

terms.meaning: The middle days of Passover and Sukkot, between the holy first and last days. Ordinary work is restricted on them, but some work is allowed to prevent a loss.
Gave up ownership of the produce, so that anyone could come and take it.

03.note: A butcher behaved disrespectfully toward Rav Tuvi bar Mattana. Abaye and Rava were appointed to the case and ostracized him. Later the butcher went and made peace with Rav Tuvi. Abaye did not know what to do: the ban had not yet lasted the usual thirty days, but the Sages wanted to buy meat at his shop. He asked Rav Idi bar Avin, who quoted Shmuel: a shofar blast puts a ban in force and a shofar blast releases it. Abaye answered that this applies to someone who ignored a money judgment, but for disrespect the ban must stay in force for thirty days.
03.why: The Gemara has just said that someone who ignores a money judgment is warned three times first, while someone who disrespects a scholar is ostracized at once. Abaye applies the same difference to lifting a ban, and the Gemara then infers his view on who may release one.

people.name: Rav Tuvi bar Mattana
people.about: The Sage the butcher treated with disrespect.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: One of the two Sages who ostracized the butcher; he weighs whether to release him.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The other Sage appointed to the case.

people.name: Rav Idi bar Avin
people.about: The Sage Abaye asks for a precedent; he quotes Shmuel.

terms.meaning: A ban placed on someone by a court or a Sage: others keep away from him until it is lifted. Excommunication is the more severe form.
A ram's horn. Its blast was sounded when a ban was announced, and could be sounded again to release it.

04.note: Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and bar Kappara were studying together and hit a difficult point of law. Rabbi Shimon said it needed his father to explain it. Bar Kappara answered, somewhat mockingly: and what can Rabbi say about this? Rabbi Shimon told his father, who became angry. When bar Kappara later came to visit, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said to him: Bar Kappara, I do not know you at all. Bar Kappara understood he had given offense, and treated himself as admonished for thirty days.
04.why: A baraita says admonition lasts seven days, and Rav Hisda said a Babylonian ban equals an admonition in the Land of Israel. The Gemara uses this story to challenge that admonition there lasts only seven days, since bar Kappara kept thirty.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; he reports bar Kappara's remark to his father.

people.name: bar Kappara
people.about: A Sage who studies with Rabbi Shimon and makes a mocking remark about his father.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; father of Rabbi Shimon, offended by bar Kappara's words.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who compares the Babylonian ban to the admonition of the Land of Israel.

terms.meaning: A milder rebuke than a formal ban. The rebuked person keeps his distance and behaves humbly for a set time.
A ban placed on someone by a court or a Sage: others keep away from him until it is lifted. Excommunication is the more severe form.

05.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi decreed that students not be taught in the marketplace: just as a thigh is kept covered, Torah should be kept hidden. Rabbi Hiyya went out and taught his nephews Rav and Rabba bar bar Hana in the marketplace. Rabbi was angered and greeted him with: Iyya, who is calling you outside? Rabbi Hiyya took himself to be admonished for thirty days. On the thirtieth day Rabbi sent for him, then sent word not to come. Rabbi Hiyya came, saying he had seen the first messenger but not the second, and Rabbi applied to him the verse about God making even a man's enemies be at peace with him. Asked why he taught in public, Rabbi Hiyya cited Wisdom cries aloud in the streets; Rabbi told him he had not understood the verse.
05.why: The Gemara is testing how long an admonition lasted in the Land of Israel; like bar Kappara before him, Rabbi Hiyya keeps thirty days. It explains Rabbi's two messages as a change of mind on whether part of a day counts as a whole day.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; he forbids teaching students in the marketplace and is angered when Rabbi Hiyya does so.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage who teaches his two nephews in the marketplace against Rabbi's decree.

people.name: Rav
people.about: One of Rabbi Hiyya's two nephews, taught in the marketplace.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's other nephew, taught alongside Rav.

terms.meaning: A milder rebuke than a formal ban. The rebuked person keeps his distance and behaves humbly for a set time.

terms.term: part of the day is like an entire day
terms.meaning: A legal principle that once a day has begun, it can count as a full day, for example the last day of a waiting period.

06.note: Mar Ukva, the Exilarch, used to accompany Shmuel to his lodgings every day, as a student honors his teacher. One day Mar Ukva was so absorbed in a court case that he did not notice Shmuel walking behind him, escorting him instead. When Mar Ukva reached his home, Shmuel said: Is it not enough for you? Release me, Master, from my obligation. Mar Ukva understood that Shmuel had taken offense, and treated himself as admonished for one day.
06.why: The Gemara asked how long an admonition lasts in Babylonia and answered one day; Mar Ukva's single day of self-imposed admonition is its proof.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: The Exilarch and chief judge, who honored Shmuel as his teacher.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage greater than Mar Ukva in Torah, who honored Mar Ukva for his office.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, who also sat as its chief judge.
A milder rebuke than a formal ban. The rebuked person keeps his distance and behaves humbly for a set time.

07.note: A woman was sitting by a path with her leg stretched out, sifting barley. A Torah scholar passed by and she did not move out of his way. He said: How rude is that woman! She came to Rav Nahman. He asked whether she had heard the word excommunication from the scholar's mouth. She said no. He told her to go and observe an admonition for one day.
07.why: The Gemara has said that an admonition in Babylonia lasts one day, proving it from Mar Ukva's case. Here a Sage gives that one-day length as a ruling.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The Sage the woman asks whether the scholar's words had put her under a ban.

terms.meaning: A milder rebuke than a formal ban. The rebuked person keeps his distance and behaves humbly for a set time.
The most severe kind of ban, cutting a person off from the community until it is lifted.

08.note: A Torah scholar had a bad reputation. Rav Yehuda was torn: the Sages needed him, but leaving him alone would desecrate God's name. Rabba bar bar Hana quoted Rabbi Yohanan: seek Torah only from a teacher who is like an angel of the Lord. So Rav Yehuda ostracized him. On his deathbed Rav Yehuda laughed when the scholar visited, glad that he had not flattered even such a man. After Rav Yehuda died, Rabbi Ami was about to release the scholar, but Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani objected, and Rabbi Zeira took the elder's rare visit as a sign. The scholar left in tears. A wasp stung him on his penis and he died. The burial caves of the pious would not accept him; the caves of the judges did.
08.why: The discussion is about who may impose a ban and how binding it is. This case upholds a ban on a needed scholar even after the Sage who imposed it had died, and the Gemara then explains why he still earned the judges' caves.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who ostracizes the scholar of bad reputation.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: Quotes Rabbi Yohanan's teaching that settles Rav Yehuda's doubt.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Sent by Rabbi Yehuda Nesia to examine the case; he does not release the ban.

people.name: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani
people.about: An elder who argues that Rav Yehuda's ban must be taken seriously.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Sees the elder's rare appearance in the study hall as a sign not to release the ban.

terms.meaning: A ban placed on someone by a court or a Sage: others keep away from him until it is lifted. Excommunication is the more severe form.
To bring God and the Torah into disrepute, for example when a known scholar behaves badly and nothing is done.

09.note: A maidservant in the house of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi saw a man striking his adult son. She declared that the man be excommunicated, because he was breaking the command not to place a stumbling block before the blind. A baraita explains that this verse speaks of a man who strikes his adult son, since the son may be provoked to strike his father back. This telling does not say what came of her ban.
09.why: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani had pointed to this maidservant's ban to argue against releasing the scholar Rav Yehuda had ostracized; the Gemara now tells the case he alluded to.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, in whose house the maidservant worked.

terms.meaning: The most severe kind of ban, cutting a person off from the community until it is lifted.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written code of Jewish law.
A Torah command (Leviticus 19:14), read here as forbidding anyone to lead another person into sin.

10.note: Reish Lakish was guarding an orchard when a man came and ate figs. Reish Lakish shouted at him, but the man paid no attention, so Reish Lakish declared him excommunicated. The man answered: on the contrary, let you be excommunicated; if I owe you money, do I owe you a ban? Reish Lakish went to the study hall, and the Sages told him the man's ban was valid and his own was not. To be released he should go to the man, but Reish Lakish did not know who he was. So they sent him to the Nasi, citing a baraita that someone banned by a person he does not know may be released by the Nasi.
10.why: Like the maidservant's ban just before it, this is a ban declared on the spot without a court. Here the Sages rule a ban used over a money matter is void, and say how to be freed from a ban when the one who imposed it is unknown.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: A Sage who was guarding an orchard for pay and banned a man who ate the figs.

terms.meaning: The most severe kind of ban, cutting a person off from the community until it is lifted.
The president of the Sanhedrin, the highest Jewish court, and the leader of the Jews in the Land of Israel.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written code of Jewish law.

11.note: Rav Yosef said that a ban cast even on a dog's tail will do its work. It was told that a dog kept eating the Sages' shoes. Not knowing who was doing it, they excommunicated the culprit. The dog's tail caught fire and burned.
11.why: The Gemara has been describing how deeply a ban takes hold of a person: Shmuel likens it to fat soaked into an oven, Reish Lakish says it enters all 248 organs. This story shows its force reaching even an animal.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who says a ban works even on a dog's tail.

terms.meaning: The most severe kind of ban, cutting a person off from the community until it is lifted.

12.note: A violent man was tormenting a Torah scholar, who came to Rav Yosef. Rav Yosef told him to ostracize the man, but the scholar said he was afraid of him. Rav Yosef told him to write out a ban against him; the scholar said he was even more afraid. So Rav Yosef told him to put the written ban in a jug, set it in a cemetery, and sound a thousand shofar blasts over forty days. The scholar did so. The jug burst and the violent man died.
12.why: It follows Rav Yosef's teaching that a ban works even on a dog's tail. Here a ban pronounced in secret, where no one hears it, still takes effect, and the Gemara explains why the shofar is sounded with a ban.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage the tormented scholar turns to, who tells him how to ban the man without being seen.

terms.meaning: A ban placed on someone by a court or a Sage: others keep away from him until it is lifted. Excommunication is the more severe form.
A ram's horn, sounded when a ban was announced. The Gemara links its name to the punishment a ban brings.

13.note: A close relative of Pinehas, Shmuel's brother, died, and Shmuel came to console him. Seeing his long nails, Shmuel asked why he did not cut them. Pinehas answered: if it were your loss, would you take it so lightly? His words came true like an error from a ruler: soon a relative of Shmuel died. When Pinehas came to console him, Shmuel took his own cut nails, threw them in Pinehas's face, and said: Do you not know that a covenant is made with the lips?
13.why: The Gemara is debating whether a mourner may cut his nails; Shmuel ruled leniently in mourning and is shown acting on it. Rabbi Yohanan's proof that spoken words shape events follows.

people.name: Pinehas
people.about: Shmuel's brother, who as a mourner let his nails grow.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who held that a mourner may cut his nails.

terms.term: a covenant is made with the lips
terms.meaning: A saying that what a person speaks aloud can bring it about, so one should be careful what one says.

terms.term: like an error from a ruler
terms.meaning: A phrase from Ecclesiastes 10:5, used here for words spoken carelessly that come true anyway.

14.note: Rava heard a man praying: grant me so-and-so as a wife. Rava told him not to pray that way: if she is meant for you, you will not lose her, and if not, you will come to deny the Lord. Later, after the man married her, Rava heard him pray that either he die before her or she die before him. Rava said to him: Did I not tell you not to pray about this?
14.why: Shmuel had said a man may betroth a woman during the Festival lest another man come first, though matches are decreed by a Divine Voice; the Gemara explains the fear as a rival praying to change the decree, and this is such a prayer.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who warns a man against praying for a particular woman.

terms.meaning: The Talmud's usual phrase for praying to God for something.

15.note: Rabbi Tzadok's father died in Ginzak, and he was told only three years later. He asked Elisha ben Avuya and the elders with him what to do, and Elisha ben Avuya told him to observe the seven-day and thirty-day mourning. Likewise, when Rabbi Ahiyya's son died abroad, Rabbi Ahiyya sat in mourning for seven and thirty days.
15.why: Rava ruled that late news of a death needs only one day of mourning; Rav Natan objected with a baraita requiring full mourning for a parent. Rava answers that this view belonged to a few individuals, citing these cases.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who cites these cases to show the strict view was held only by individuals.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: Learned of his father's death three years late.

people.name: Elisha ben Avuya
people.about: The Sage who told Rabbi Tzadok to observe full mourning.

people.name: Rabbi Ahiyya
people.about: A Sage who sat seven and thirty days of mourning for his son who died abroad.

terms.meaning: The two stages of Jewish mourning: an intense first week, and a lighter period lasting to the thirtieth day.

16.note: Rav was Rabbi Hiyya's nephew twice over, the son of his brother and of his sister. When Rav came to the Land of Israel, Rabbi Hiyya asked him: Is your father alive? Rav answered: Is my mother alive? Rabbi Hiyya asked: Is your mother alive? Rav answered: Is my father alive? Rabbi Hiyya understood that both had died. He told his servant to take off his shoes, and then to carry his clothes after him to the bathhouse.
16.why: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Ahiyya mourned seven and thirty days for late news, since Rabbi Hiyya here mourned briefly. It learns that late news needs one day of mourning and that part of a day counts as a day, then says Hiyya and Ahiyya are two people.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's nephew, son of both his brother and his sister, who avoids saying outright that his parents died.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: Rav's uncle, who works out from Rav's answers that his brother and sister have died.

terms.meaning: A mourner may not wear leather shoes, so removing them is a first act of mourning.

17.note: Mar Ukva's brother-in-law, the son of his father-in-law, died, and Mar Ukva meant to observe the seven-day and thirty-day mourning for him. Rav Huna came to his house, found him mourning, and said: Do you want to eat mourners' food? The Sages said that a man mourns out of honor for his wife only for his father-in-law or mother-in-law.
17.why: The Gemara is asking when one must join a relative's mourning. Rav Huna's limit is then backed by two baraitot, read as separating a wife's parents from her other relatives.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: A Sage who began mourning for his wife's brother.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who tells Mar Ukva he need not mourn for his brother-in-law.

terms.meaning: The meals eaten by people in mourning. Rav Huna is asking, in effect, whether Mar Ukva wants to take on mourning he is not required to keep.

18.note: Ameimar's grandson, his son's son, died, and Ameimar tore his garment over him. When his son came, Ameimar tore his garment again in his son's presence. Then he remembered that he had torn it while sitting, so he stood up and tore it again standing.
18.why: The Gemara has been discussing mourning alongside a relative who is in mourning, as Ameimar does for his son. Rav Ashi then asks him for the source that tearing must be done standing.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: A Sage whose grandson died and who tore his garment three times.

terms.meaning: A Jewish mourning rite: on hearing of a close relative's death, the mourner tears his clothing.

19.note: Rabbi Yosei's son died in the town of Tzippori. Rabbi Yosei went into the study hall and taught there for the entire day.
19.why: A baraita lists what a mourner may not do, among them work, bathing and studying Torah, but adds that if the public needs him he need not hold back from teaching. Rabbi Yosei's day of teaching is its example.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage who taught in the study hall on the day his son died.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written code of Jewish law.
The house of study, where the Sages taught Torah to students and the public.

20.note: When Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai's son died, he went into the study hall. Rabbi Hananya ben Akavya came in and sat beside him. Rabbi Yehuda whispered his lecture to Rabbi Hananya ben Akavya, who whispered it to the disseminator, and the disseminator announced it to the public.
20.why: Rav told the mourning Rabba bar bar Hana that a mourner who teaches may not have an interpreter beside him. The Gemara asks how he can be heard, and answers with this case.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai
people.about: A Sage who taught in the study hall after his son died.

people.name: Rabbi Hananya ben Akavya
people.about: A Sage who sat beside him and passed his words on.

terms.meaning: The speaker who repeated a Sage's lecture aloud to the crowd, since the Sage spoke quietly.
